explanations.explanation: That's the plot twist, friend. You hear that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown, and you brace for a cold shoulder, and then the Galileans welcome Him. John adds that they had seen all the great things He had done in Jerusalem at the feast, for they had gone there as well. Hometown crowds can surprise you.

I get why you'd go there. That line about no honor at home sounds like a door slamming. But John 4:45 says the Galileans welcomed Him. They had been at the feast in Jerusalem and had seen what He did there.
Jerusalem it is. The Galileans had gone to the feast, and they saw the great things Jesus did there. So when He showed up in Galilee, they weren't hearing it secondhand. They were there.

Bethlehem is a good Bible town, but it's not in this verse. John 4:45 says the Galileans saw all those great things in Jerusalem at the feast, because they had gone there as well. Big feast, big city, front-row seats.

Samaria is close, since Jesus had just spent two days there (John 4:40). But the verse points to a different place. The Galileans saw those great things in Jerusalem, at the feast they had traveled to as well.
Cana, the water into wine town. John doesn't just say Jesus came to Cana. He says He came once again, to the place where He had turned the water into wine. That's a place with a history.
Feeding a crowd with bread isn't the moment John points back to here. John 4:46 says Cana is the place where He had turned the water into wine. Nice thinking, though, friend.

That's a real story, but it's a different one (John 9:1-7). John 4:46 ties Cana to something else: it's where Jesus had turned the water into wine. Good Bible instincts, friend, but that's not the one John points to here.

Begs, friend. That's the word John uses. John 4:47 says the official went and begged Jesus to come down and heal his son. He's a royal official, and he's down to begging. That tells you how badly he needs help.
Orders sounds like something a royal official might do, doesn't it? But John 4:47 says he went and begged. He was a royal official, and he begged.
Nobody's handing over a contract here. John 4:47 says the official went and begged Jesus to come down and heal his son. No offer, no deal, just a father asking.

True, friend. John 4:47 says the official's son was about to die. It's the same verse where the official goes and begs Jesus to come down and heal him. I think a father hears that and just starts moving.
Oh, I wish it were, friend. But John 4:47 says the boy was about to die. That's the weight this father is carrying when he goes looking for Jesus.

explanations.answer: Says to come down before his child dies
explanations.explanation: He doesn't flinch. He says, "Sir, come down before my child dies." (John 4:49) Jesus just said something that could have stung, and the father keeps his eyes on his boy. I think that's a man who has one thing on his mind.

explanations.answer: Argues that he already believes in Him
explanations.explanation: That would be a natural thing to say, but John never gives us that. The official says, "Sir, come down before my child dies." (John 4:49) No debate, no defending himself. Just the request again.

explanations.answer: Asks Him to show a sign right there
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask for a show. John 4:49 has him say, "Sir, come down before my child dies." He's asking Jesus to come to his boy, not to perform for the room.

explanations.answer: Takes Jesus at His word and leaves
explanations.explanation: John says it plainly: the man took Jesus at His word and departed (John 4:50). Jesus hadn't agreed to come down, and the father went anyway. All he had were the words "Your son will live." and he headed home with them.

explanations.answer: Waits until Jesus agrees to come
explanations.explanation: He had been asking Jesus to come down, so I see why you'd pick this. But Jesus said, "Go," and John 4:50 says the man took Jesus at His word and departed. He didn't stand around waiting for a different answer.

explanations.answer: Sends a servant ahead to check first
explanations.explanation: No scouting report here. John 4:50 says the man took Jesus at His word and departed. The servants do show up in the story, but they come to meet him on the road, not the other way around.
I know the dread is real, but this one goes the other way. The servants meet him with the news that his boy was alive (John 4:51). Not worse, not holding on. Alive.
False, and thank goodness. John 4:51 says his servants met him on the way with the news that his boy was alive. That's the word he needed on that road.

explanations.answer: What hour his son got better
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. John 4:52 says he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered. Good news landed, and he still wanted to know exactly when it happened. I think that's a man who is connecting dots.

explanations.answer: Who came to heal his son
explanations.explanation: It's a fair question, but it's not the one John records. John 4:52 says he inquired as to the hour his son had recovered. The time is what he's after.

explanations.answer: If the fever might come back
explanations.explanation: A worried dad could ask that, no doubt. But John 4:52 says he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered. He's asking about the moment it happened, not what might happen next.

explanations.answer: It's when Jesus said his son will live
explanations.explanation: The seventh hour matched. The father realized it was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, "Your son will live." (John 4:53) Same hour, no gap. And John says he and all his household believed.

explanations.answer: It's when he set out to find Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's a tidy guess, but John doesn't say it. John 4:53 says the father realized it was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, "Your son will live." That's the hour that clicked.

explanations.answer: It's when the boy's fever first began
explanations.explanation: The fever shows up in the story, but the text points elsewhere. The servants say it left the boy at the seventh hour, and John 4:53 says the father realized that was the very hour Jesus told him, "Your son will live." The hour is about the fever leaving, not starting.
Household. John 4:53 says he and all his household believed. It wasn't only the dad who walked away changed. The whole home came along.
Neighbors would make for a nice crowd, but John doesn't mention them. The text says he and all his household believed (John 4:53). That means everyone under his roof.
John never brings soldiers into this scene. He says the man was a royal official, and that he and all his household believed (John 4:53). The answer is the people living in his home.

Second. John 4:54 calls it the second sign Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee. The first was at Cana, when He turned the water into wine (John 2:11). Cana got both of them, and I'm a little jealous.

The first sign was already done. John 2:11 says Jesus did it at Cana in Galilee, when He turned the water into wine. So John 4:54 says this healing was the second sign after He came from Judea into Galilee.
Not yet, friend. John 4:54 says this was now the second sign Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee. Second is the number John gives.
